pronunciation_note: Pronounced 'wa' when used as a particle, not 'ha'

definitions.explanation: Marks the topic of a sentence—what the sentence is about. The topic is often (but not always) the grammatical subject. は sets up what the speaker wants to comment on, and the rest of the sentence provides information about that topic.

Indicates contrast with something else, either stated or implied. When は is used on an element that would normally take a different particle (like を or に), it often adds a contrastive nuance: 'as for X (as opposed to something else)...'

particle_contrasts.explanation: は marks the TOPIC (known information); が marks NEW information or identifies the subject

examples.ha_example: {田中|たなか}さんは{来|き}ましたか。→ はい、{来|き}ました。
examples.ha_note: は marks known topic—we're asking about Tanaka specifically

examples.ga_example: {誰|だれ}が{来|き}ましたか。→ {田中|たなか}さんが{来|き}ました。
examples.ga_note: が marks new information in the answer

key_points: は marks OLD/KNOWN information (topic); が marks NEW information
In 'who/what' questions, the answer uses が (new info)
In yes/no questions about someone, use は (known topic)
が is used in subordinate clauses, not は

information_structure.description: Understanding new vs. old information is key to は/が

principles.point: は marks what is already known or established in context
principles.example: {私|わたし}は{学生|がくせい}です
principles.explanation: The speaker is known; we're providing new info about them

principles.point: が introduces new information or identifies
principles.example: あ、{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っている
{肉|にく}は{食|た}べます（が、{魚|さかな}は{食|た}べません）
principles.explanation: As for meat, I eat [it] (but as for fish, I don't)

fixed_patterns.example: {象|ぞう}は{鼻|はな}が{長|なが}い
fixed_patterns.example_english: As for elephants, their noses are long

fixed_patterns.example: {学生|がくせい}ではありません
{今日|きょう}は{昨日|きのう}ほど{暑|あつ}くない
fixed_patterns.example_english: Today is not as hot as yesterday

examples.japanese: {私|わたし}は{学生|がくせい}です。
{今日|きょう}は{天気|てんき}がいいです。
{田中|たなか}さんは{先生|せんせい}で、{山田|やまだ}さんは{医者|いしゃ}です。
examples.english: Tanaka-san is a teacher, and Yamada-san is a doctor.

examples.japanese: {象|ぞう}は{鼻|はな}が{長|なが}い。これはみんな{知|し}っていることだ。
examples.english: Elephants have long trunks. Everyone knows this.
I like this one. (implying: but not that one)
I do eat fish. (implying: but not meat)

examples.japanese: {読|よ}みはするが、{書|か}くのは{苦手|にがて}だ。
examples.english: I can read (it), but I'm not good at writing.

examples.japanese: {映画|えいが}は{見|み}ましたが、{本|ほん}はまだ{読|よ}んでいません。
examples.english: I watched the movie, but I haven't read the book yet.

examples.japanese: {平日|へいじつ}は{忙|いそが}しいですが、{週末|しゅうまつ}は{時間|じかん}があるので、ぜひ{遊|あそ}びに{来|き}てください。
examples.english: I'm busy on weekdays, but I have time on weekends, so please come visit.

common_mistakes.explanation: Question words ({誰|だれ}, {何|なに}, どれ) take が, not は

common_mistakes.incorrect: {田中|たなか}さんは{買|か}った{本|ほん}
common_mistakes.correct: {田中|たなか}さんが{買|か}った{本|ほん}
common_mistakes.explanation: Use が (not は) for subjects inside relative clauses

common_mistakes.incorrect: {窓|まど}から{鳥|とり}は{見|み}えます
common_mistakes.correct: {窓|まど}から{鳥|とり}が{見|み}えます
common_mistakes.explanation: When describing what you notice/perceive, use が

notes: は is pronounced 'wa' when used as a particle, not 'ha'. This is one of the most important particles in Japanese. The difference between は (topic) and が (subject) is one of the most challenging aspects for learners. Generally: は marks old/known information or the topic of discussion; が marks new information or identifies the subject when making a neutral description or answering 'who/what' questions.
